key_concept: Alkyne reduction stereochemistry: Lindlar's catalyst gives the cis-alkene (syn addition) and Na/liq. $NH_3$ gives the trans-alkene (anti addition); ionic HBr addition and peroxide (radical) HBr addition put Br on different carbons.
steps: K: $Ph-C\equiv C-Me \xrightarrow{H_2,\ Lindlar}$ syn addition of $H_2$ gives cis-1-phenylprop-1-ene, $Ph-CH=CH-CH_3$ (cis).
L: $Ph-C\equiv C-Me \xrightarrow{Na/liq.\ NH_3}$ Birch-type anti reduction gives trans-1-phenylprop-1-ene, $Ph-CH=CH-CH_3$ (trans).
K and L have the same connectivity and differ only in the arrangement about the $C=C$ bond, so they are geometrical (cis–trans) isomers. Option (1) is correct.
M: K + HBr (ionic addition). $H^+$ adds so that the more stable benzylic carbocation $Ph-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_2CH_3$ forms. $Br^-$ then attacks it, giving $Ph-CHBr-CH_2-CH_3$ (1-bromo-1-phenylpropane).

N: L + HBr with benzoyl peroxide (radical, anti-Markovnikov). $Br^\bullet$ adds so that the more stable benzylic radical $Ph-\dot{C}H-CHBr-CH_3$ forms. This gives $Ph-CH_2-CHBr-CH_3$ (2-bromo-1-phenylpropane).
M and N have Br on different carbons, so they are position (structural) isomers. They are neither geometrical isomers nor stereoisomers, and neither has a $C=C$ bond.
final_answer: Option (1): K and L are geometrical isomers
why_not_others: K and L are achiral cis/trans alkenes, so they cannot be enantiomers. M and N differ in the position of Br (C-1 vs C-2), so they are positional isomers, not geometrical isomers or stereoisomers.
common_trap: Students often think the cis/trans geometry of K and L carries over to M and N, and so call M and N stereoisomers. In fact, adding HBr destroys the double bond, and the two addition modes place Br on different carbons.
time_saving_tip: Recall 'Lindlar → cis, Na/NH$_3$ → trans': this immediately makes K and L geometrical isomers, and you can mark option (1) without working out M and N.
